summary:
FireSync is a fire record from two satellite generations made consistent and comparable.

We developed a web app and data pipeline that merge NASA’s MODIS (2003–present) and VIIRS (2012–present) fire hotspots into one comparable record. It is designed to run for any country and Argentina is our first fully worked region.

VIIRS sees small fires that MODIS misses, so the raw record jumps around 3.5 times when VIIRS arrives. The application counts burn days on a 10 km grid and rescales the MODIS data to VIIRS-equivalent values, using factors fitted for each month and region. To test the harmonized MODIS data, every year from 2012 to 2020 was left out once, one after another, the factors fitted on the remaining years, and then the harmonized MODIS data alone was used to predict what VIIRS measured in the missing year. The predicted yearly total number of burn days was typically within 4.8% of the real total number of burn days. We also added a burning activity calendar where users can pick a region and date range, see patterns, unusual months and critical periods, and download the data as a CSV file.

This solution is necessary because MODIS is nearing the end of its life. Without harmonization, every long fire record breaks at the sensor change. Once harmonized, burning in Argentina is about 28% lower in recent years, not higher. FireSync also adds a forecast so fire managers can prepare.
details:
The two fire sensors operated by NASA, MODIS and VIIRS, see fire very differently. MODIS has 1 km pixels, whereas VIIRS has 375 m pixels and detects small fires that MODIS misses. Simply joining the datasets makes burning appear to rise 3.5 times when VIIRS begins in 2012. That jump comes from how the sensors work, not from an actual rise in fires.

We solved this by standardizing both datasets into one format (timestamps, local dates, confidence levels, fire type). We applied the same quality criteria to the data from both MODIS and VIIRS, flagging non-vegetation sources, low-confidence detections, duplicates and static heat sources such as gas flares, and leaving them out of the counts. We then divided Argentina into a common 10 km × 10 km grid and gave every detection a Grid_ID.

Instead of comparing hotspot counts, we compare whether a grid cell recorded fire on a given day. We call the days on which a fire was recorded in a grid cell burn days. This makes the sensors comparable despite their pixel sizes. For calibration we used data from the Aqua satellite (MODIS) and the Suomi NPP satellite (VIIRS) from 2012 to 2020, because the two pass over the same regions at nearly the same time. For each calendar month and each of 12 fire regions we calculated a factor, k, defined as VIIRS burn days per MODIS burn day. For Argentina as a whole it ranges from about 2.7 to 4.3 through the year. The MODIS-only years (2003 to early 2012) are multiplied by k to give VIIRS-equivalent values.

To test the method, we left out each year from 2012 to 2020 in turn, fitted k on the remaining years, and predicted the left-out year’s burn days from that year’s MODIS data alone. The prediction was typically within 4.8% of the burn days VIIRS actually recorded. We could not test on 2003–2011, because VIIRS did not exist then. We did not fit k on 2021–2026, because Aqua’s orbit has been drifting in those years, but we used 2021–2025 as an extra check. There the method was within 11%. Once harmonized, burning in Argentina is about 28% lower in recent years, the opposite of what the raw record suggests.

Our web app, FireSync, lets a user pick a region, a date range and a kind of fire (day, night, intense, large, multi-day). It then shows a burning activity calendar, anomalies against the normal for each month, the critical period, the most unusual months, and a map of where fire burned for that selection. The selection downloads as a CSV file. It also gives a forecast for the next 1, 3, 6 and 12 months, a Monte Carlo simulation of 20,000 possible futures for each, and a ranking of the regions facing the most fire.

MODIS is nearing the end of its life. Without harmonization, the long historical record cannot be compared with modern data. FireSync gives responders, scientists and land managers a trend they can trust, and the method can be repeated for any country.

We built it with Python (pandas, NumPy), Power BI and DAX, JavaScript, D3.js, HTML/CSS, GitHub and Vercel.
